Question: Is there actually a physical border out there on the prairie between America and Canada? Can you just walk across in many places and maybe not even know which country you are in?
Answer: No, the border is the 49th parallel an imaginary dotted line on the map, and it gets a little tenuous in places, so it is easy to end up in the wrong country by mistake. The sign here warns you that this is the junction between Montana Border Road and Alberta Highway 500, so you have to clear customs at the port of Entry of Sweetgrass Montana / Coutts Alberta, which is only a few dozen miles or kilometres away. Further down the road, you just have to know you are in the US, and not in Canada. Notice the difference, or lack thereof. They saved taxpayer dollars by only building one road, not paving it, and not putting in a border wall or fence… or even a ditch. And then you arrive at the Port of Sweetgrass/Coutts, the major port of entry in Alberta US Interstate 15 meets Alberta Highway 4 here, which eventually connects to the Alaska Highway. The main North American railway tracks run through, while the Montana Border Road ends and Alberta Highway 500 goes wandering around Alberta somewhere. Don’t get lost. During the Covid 19 pandemic, one family took advantage of the neighbourly lack of formal border controls to hold a cross border wedding in this area.

Question: Did anyone in pre-Civil War America ever try to get the slaves to do industrial work? If not, did people think that this would be too immoral (the factory conditions was after all very bad at the time) or was it simply against the plantation culture?
Answer: The great British economist Adam Smith, in his defining work on captalism “The Wealth of Nations”, published in 1776 examined this problem in detail. He also found that the plantation system was an inefficient use of land compared to the homesteading system, and that slavery was an inefficient use of labor since free men would look after feeding, clothing, and sheltering themselves,, and keep coming back for more as long as the wages were competitive. He found that slaves could not be trusted to do industrial work because they kept trying to escape, would not maintain the machines properly, and do as little work as possible, while free men would keep coming back and working harder to try to make more money. The machines themselves just wanted fuel and some oil, and would work 24/7 without complaint, unlike the men. The factory work in the Northern US, and in fact in England, paid better than working as a slave or landless peasant, which often did not involve being paid at all. A factory worker in America had a chance to learn enough to start his own business and put most of the money in his own pocket. Many were ambitious enough to try, and enough succeeded at it to encourage others to follow. The workers also had the opportunity to quit their jobs and head West if they didn’t like the conditions in the East. My own ancestors came from Europe, worked in the mines and forests for someone else, and then worked building the railroads heading West, before they homesteaded the land in the West — where they got free land. After that, it was up to them how hard they wanted to work. Most of them had to work unbelievably hard — sunrise to sunset, after which they would get ready for the next day’s work. And if they went bankrupt farming, they just went back to working for someone else. There were always job opportunities because America had a chronic labor shortage — there just weren’t enough people to take advantage of all the natural resources the New World presented them with.

Question: Why were blacks the only race made into slaves?
Answer: Just about every race known to man has been made into slaves at one point or another in human history. For instance, Arab slave traders captured about 1 milion white Christian Europeans and sold them as slaves in North Africa, reversing the usual picture of slavery. The Vikings commonly captured Slavs in their raids through Central Europe and sold them as slaves in the Arab countries, which is where the English names “slave” and “Slavs” originated. And then in an interesting bit of trivia, there are the Slavey people of Canada’s Northwest Territories, who were so called because they were often taken as slaves by their southern neighbours, the Cree. They originate from around Great Slave Lake the deepest lake in North America at 614 m (2,014 ft), and the tenth-largest lake in the world by area. As the French explorers dealt directly with the Cree traders, the large lake was referred to as "Grand lac des Esclaves" which was eventually translated into English as "Great Slave Lake" The Cree used to meet to trade them at Lesser Slave Lake in Northern Alberta, whiich is the second largest lake in Alberta and drains into the NWT via the Lesser Slave River — a main Cree trading route to the north, which they used long before the White Europeans came. The lake shares its name with the First Nations peoples of the Dene family which were called Slavey by their enemies the Cree. The Slavey actually called themselves “Dene Tha” which means “Ordinary People” in their language. I guess the point I am making is that at the time of the American slave trade, the vast majority of slaves in Canada were native people being held captive by other native people, who occasionally sold them to white Europeans. Black slaves were relatively rare in Canada, and the slave trade was abolished in Canada around 1800, as a direct but unexpected consequence of the American revolution. From a personal perspective, I used to work in the town of Slave Lake - stayed at a First Nations hotel and filled up at their truck stop. Some people think the name should be changed, but I am not a believer in rewriting history to erase historical facts. Particularly since the average member of this tribe is now a millionaire - they did really well on their hotel chain.

Question: How did the Europeans infect American Indians with smallpox, but not have smallpox themselves? How did they gain immunity if their parents or grandparents had it? How does that work?
Answer: Smallpox was not confined to American Indians. It killed an estimated 400,000 Europeans each year in the 18th century, including five reigning European monarchs. Most Europeans became infected during their lifetimes, and between 20 and 60% of all those infected—and over 80% of infected children—died from the disease. Overall, about 30% of people infected with smallpox died, presenting a severe selection pressure on the survivors. This produced a form of herd immunity against the disease since it did not spread rapidly among populations where large numbers of people had already had it. Herd immunity occurs when a significant portion of a population becomes immune to an infectious disease and the risk of spread from person to person decreases; those who are not immune are indirectly protected because ongoing disease spread is very small. The advantage that European settlers had over the Native Indians was that most Europeans had already had smallpox before they came to the New World and so were immune or protected by herd immunity, whereas it killed 80 to 90% of the Native Indians who were getting it for the first time. Indigenous populations of regions where smallpox was non-native, were rapidly and greatly reduced by smallpox (along with other introduced diseases) during periods of initial foreign contact. In 1520 a group of Spanish arrived in Mexico, bringing smallpox with them. For more than 200 years, smallpox affected all new world populations, mostly without intentional European transmission. Once introduced to Mexico, smallpox killed most of the Aztec army and 25% of the overall population — The Spaniards said that they could not walk through the streets of Tenochtitlán without stepping on the bodies of smallpox victims. Smallpox also spread rapidly through the Inca empire even before the Spanish invaders first arrived. The Incan Emperor Huayna Capac, his successor, and most of the other Inca leaders died of it and within a few years smallpox killed between 60% and 90% of the Inca population, leading to an easy Spanish victory. As it had done elsewhere, the virus wiped out entire population groups of Native North Americans. During the 1770s, smallpox killed at least 30% of the Northwestern Natives. The smallpox epidemic of 1780–1782 brought drastic depopulation among the Plains Indians, with death rates up to 95% of some tribes. This epidemic is a classic instance of European immunity and non-European vulnerability. However in Canada, between 1702 and 1703, nearly a quarter of the population of Quebec city died due to a smallpox epidemic, illustrating European vulnerability. For the most part smallpox spread from Native to Native rather than from European to Native. The stories of smallpox being spread on infected blankets are mostly myths since smallpox is an airborne disease which can be spread just by talking to an infected person, but it doesn’t last long outside the human body. One story claims that during the French and Indian Wars, at Fort Pitt the British gave as gifts two blankets from the smallpox hospital to two Delaware Indian delegates. However, the dignitaries were met again later and they seemingly hadn't contracted smallpox.

Answer: cleaner and less littered like the United States ??? What cities and states have you been in? Compare to Detroit today When I was born 76 years ago, Detroit had a population of 1.8 million while Toronto had a population of 1.2 million. At the same time, Calgary grew from 130,000 to 1.6 million, or over 12 times in population. I spent most of my life in a construction zone and it has accelerated since I left. Question: A sixth grade teacher is teaching my child about evolution and that the earth is billions of years old. I do not want this taught to my child because it goes against our religious conviction. What do I say to the teacher to accomplish this?
Answer: The trouble with keeping children in a blissful state of ignorance about the past is that when they grow up and learn the true facts, they begin to lose all faith in anything you told them. I remember a friend of mine in university who was brought up in such a culture. He posed a question to one of his professors about the “missing link” between ape and man. The professor took out some skulls from his cabinet, lined them up in a row from Australopithicus (the South African Ape) at one end to modern human at the other, and said, “Where in this row is your ‘missing link’?’” He was crushed because he realized a lot of things had been left out of his education, and began to question everything about what he had learned from his elders. Somewhat who had a more complete education than my college buddy would have taken it in his stride. Myself, being the questioning little snot I was, I once brought a dinosaur bone I had found to Sunday School and asked them to explain what it was and how it got there. They couldn’t, so I realized I was looking in the wrong place for answers. I really needed to be looking in the paleontology books instead. BTW, they later built the largest museum of paleontology 15 minutes drive from where I grew up, so all I needed was a pair of glasses to find dinosaur bones lying on the ground. There was a shortage of religous artifacts, though, and the only ones we had were left by the First Nations — which had nothing to do with anything in the Bible. Once you get into science, travel a bit, and look around, the pieces all start to fall into place. Why is there a vertical mile of sedimentary rock in the Grand Canyon? Why are there seashells at the top of the Rocky Mountains? Why is the sky blue? — all questions the Bible does not answer. It took a lot more than 6000 years for it to happen. OTOH, if I have any religious questions, I will look in the Bible for answers since science does not have them. However, there are several different versions of every story in Genesis, so you cannot take them literally down to the finest detail. They are a moral guide, not history or science in the generally accepted sense. This is why churches used to appoint a “devil’s advocate” — to take the opposite stance and immunize religious scholars against contrary opinions.

Question: Why do gun nuts keep saying that the AR-15 is not an assault rifle when it was originally designed for and issued to military servicemen? Do they not know the origins of this weapon that they defend?
Answer: Well they are confused by the fact that the original AR-15 was designed to be a lightweight assault rifle by ArmLite (hence the AR prefix), but the rights were later sold to Colt, which marketed it to the US military as the M-16 and continues to do so under a variety of model names. However, Colt later marketed a semi-automatic-only version to civilians under the trademark Colt AR-15. The modern AR-15 is more of a modular rifle concept than a particular rifle and is marketed by a variety of manufacturers of rifles and parts. The original version of the AR-15, though, was a true assault rifle — a name first given to the German Stg 44, the world’s first assault rifle, by US military intelligence during WW2. The “Stg” stands for “Sturmgewehr” or “Storm rifle”. Unfortunately the US army didn’t realize what the Germans had done until they ran into the Russian interpretation of it, the AK-47, in Vietnam for which it was much better suited than the US army M-14. Today, the term assault rifle is used to define firearms sharing the same basic characteristics as the Stg 44, to wit: Unlike “assault rifle”, the term “assault weapon” has no particular meaning, which confuses the issues. However, the original AR-15 was an assault rifle, the current trade name “Colt AR-15” is the semi-automatic version of it. However, the AR-15 platform is modular, so it can be converted to everything from a varmit gun useful for shooting small game to a light machine gun. In the United States, selective-fire rifles are legally defined as "machine guns”. It should be noted that, given its military heritage, even the semi-automatic version of the AR-15 is quite lethal. It is capable of firing two rounds per second, and hitting targets 300 metres or more away, whereas when the Second Amendment was written, the average muzzle loading gun could only fire a round every minute or two, and was extremely inaccurate. You could seldom hit anything at long range with it, hence the Revolutionary phrase “Don’t fire until you see the whites of their eyes.”

Question: When gas prices drop suddenly and by a lot, does the owner of the individual station have to absorb the loss, or is there some other agreement with the fuel supplier?
Answer: Unbeknownst to most people, the profit margins on fuel at service stations are very small, and sometimes non-existant — they make their money from overpriced snacks and car washes rather than gasoline and diesel fuel. When gas prices drop suddenly, it’s fish or cut bait time for the fuel suppliers. They either match the competitors’ prices to keep competitive, or they don’t. If they run out of refinery capacity they will not bother to match the price and you will see fuel stations across the street from each other with substantially different prices. Fuel suppliers have big refineries which are expensive to operate at less than full capacity, so they keep track of prices closely and have people cruising the streets looking at the gas station signs, plus which the fuel station owners have binoculars so they can look at their competitors signs. Then the fuel suppliers adjust their wholesale prices to the stations to match the competition because the station owners don’t have any wiggle room to do so. Gasoline and diesel fuel are fungible — They are basically all the same for any given product, so the difference is really only in the additives they put in it. Thus there is something approximating a free market, and in a free market there is only one price — the market price, which is determined by supply vs. demand. If the supply goes up or the demand goes down, the price goes down, sometimes by a lot. The price though is “sticky” in the downward direction, and much faster to move up than down. The name of the company on the fuel stations is frequently not the same as the company supplying the fuel, and companies will buy fuel from each other and put in their own addtives if they have to. Tanker trucks from fuel suppliers will drive around from station to station and put the correct additives in for the company whose name is on the station, but the fuel is all the same. Unbeknownst to most Americans, the second biggest oil refiner in the US is Motiva Enterprises which you seldom see on station signs but operates as a distributor of Shell and 76 other branded gasolines and is owned by (drum roll please) Saudi Aramco, the state oil company of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia — Now do you feel you have been left out of the information loop somehow? Ultimately, the price of fuel depends on the price of crude oil, with a month or two delay for the oil to move through the system. Saudi Arabia and the other OPEC countries are trying to create a monopoly on oil and charge a higher price, but unfortunately for them those pesky Canadians have taken advantage of the opportunity to make sales by the simple expedient of undercutting their prices, but the monopolists do have the advantage that the gullible greens and Democrats are blocking pipelines so Canadian oil can’t get through the system to the refineries. OPEC oil comes in on seaborne tankers. California is a worst case scenario since there aren’t any oil or fuel pipelines to California from either Canada or the other US states If Californians are wondering why their gasoline is $1 or so higher than the rest of the US — It is the only state that takes a substantial amount of OPEC oil any more.

Question: How are mineral resources like oil managed to prevent issues such as a neighbor drilling and extracting resources from my land? For example, if I find oil on my property, how is it ensured that my neighbor cannot drill and take my resources?
Answer: You can drill an offset well near the property boundary and produce the oil before he does. Oil is mobile, and if you are sharing the same underground pool of it, it will flow toward his producing wells unless you drill your own wells in the pool. Alternatively, you can sign a pooling agreement to share the revenue from his wells, but in return you have to share the costs involved in drilling the wells. Be prepared to bring a lot of money to the negotiating table. Case in point: The Alberta provincial government sold oil leases on provincial land immediately adjacent to a national park, and oil companies started drilling them. The Canadian federal government sued the Alberta government for a share of the royalties on the grounds that some of the oil came from under the park. The judges ruled that the only way the federal government could get a share of the money was to drill wells near the boundary INSIDE the national park. It was a “use it or lose it” situation and since the federal government would not do it, it lost it. Since the provincial government was drilling oil wells in its own provincial parks, it didn’t see why the federal government couldn’t do the same in its national parks. It just disguised them to look more like trees than oil wells. Working for an oil company, I designed a computer system to identify places where we needed to drill offset wells. It located all the wells drilled by other companies immediately adjacent to our non-producing leases and got the production rates for them from our databases and government files. Then it created a list of the leases in descending order based on other companies’ nearby production, for use by the exploration department. They would go out, shoot seismic on the leases, find the pool boundaries, and decide whether or not and where to drill. This required access to information that the average Joe does not have. The damn program could even find production data for “tight holes” — wells where the information is supposed to be secret. Thats what happens when you put some artificial intelligence into a program, and it figures out what to do by itself.

Question: In regions which spans a wide area crossing the meridians of neighboring time zones, like Europe, do people from east till west all work at a 9 to 5 schedule, or does one side do 8 to 4 and the other side 9 to 5?
Answer: It depends on the industry. For instance, the North American natural gas industry operates on Central Clock Time (CCT) because it crosses multiple time zones from Atlantic to Pacific Oceans. CCT is Central Standard Time (CST) or Central Daylight Savings Time (CDT), whichever is in effect on any given day. The North American Energy Standards Board “Gas Day” is 9:00 AM to 9:00 AM CCT, which is 7:00 to 7:00 AM Pacific Clock Time on the Pacific Coast at LA and 10:00 to 10:00 AM Eastern Clock Time on the Atlantic Coast at NYC. It is also 9:00 to 9:00 AM Central Clock Time in the main gas producing state of Texas and 8:00 to 8:00 Mountain Clock Time in the main gas producing province of Alberta. The banks use a “Business Day” which opens at 8:00 AM CCT and closes at 5:00 PM CCT. This means 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM in NYC and Toronto, the main banking centres in the US and Canada repectively. In Canada it means that gas sellers and investment bankers in Calgary work the same time as gas buyers and investment bankers in Toronto. They just work 9 to 5 eastern time in Toronto and 7 to 3 mountain time in Calgary. In fact, since they are the two main head office centres in Canada, offices in Calgary generally run 2 hours ahead of Toronto, 2700 km to the east, which gives Calgarians a couple of extra hours to go golfing or skiing after work (there is a ski hill inside the city limits). The flip side is that it is rather cold and dark when they get to work on winter mornings. They get used to it.

Question: What do you do when a client refuses to pay you for a plumbing service provided?
Answer: Well, you can place a mechanic’s lien on the property and take him to small claims court to recover the money. You might have to wait a while to get your money, but small claims court is rather cheap and mostly costs you time. The owner of a property may want to resolve a mechanic’s lien as soon as possible because a property typically cannot be sold while a lien is in effect. Mechanic’s liens generally have a higher priority than other forms of debt, so if he wants to sell or mortgage it, you have him by the short and curlies. The mechanic’s lien was first developed by Thomas Jefferson. It is called a mechanic's lien because construction workers were referred to as mechanics (or people who work with their hands) in those days. You really want to put the lien on as soon as possible. Construction companies get upset when aware tradespeople get wind that a bankruptcy may be coming and they get hit with an avalanche of them, which ties up their properties. Extreme case in point: my father was doing some backhoe work on an oil well, when he got word that the prime contractor was going to go bankrupt, so he was proactive and filed a mechanic’s lien on the oil well ASAP. There were 400 people they owed money to, but only my Dad and 3 others got paid in full. Since I was workiing as a business analyst for an oil company, I told him: “Nice going Dad, you put the oil company drilling the well in breach of contract with its partners”. There was probably a joint venture agreement on developing the oil well, and there was probably a clause in it that said something like, “The operating parter shall keep the property free and clear of all liens and incumbrances.” Oil companies take it seriously because it affects the value of their assets and loans. In a situation like this, the oil company partners took the money they owed the prime contractor and just gave it to my Dad in return for lifting the lien. If anybody had any objections, their team of high-priced lawers stood willing, able, and keen to accept their call and see them in court. Other case in point: A young lady I met at a party told me that at 16 her father had given her a job answering the phone at his electrical company. She got bored and started digging through the accounts recievable, and found to her horror that one company owed her father $60,000 and wasn’t paying. So she called up the owner and threatened to repossess his light fixtures and switches under a mechanic’s lien. She frightened him so badly he paid up the next day. When he found out it was a 16 year old girl who did this to him, he wanted to hire her to collect from people who owed him money. When I met her she was working for the sherriff’s department doing repossesions. Side note to the above: She later had 3 children by the boyfriend who brought her to the party. Then he found another girlfriend, broke up with her, and refused to pay child support. Well, good luck with that, buddy, she works for the freaking SHERRIFF’S DEPARTMENT and has the fighting spirit of a pit bull. Last time I heard, she had been seen chasing him and his private airplane around an airport runway in her car, trying to seize it for non-payment of child support.

Question: Why is the gap between the physical strength of men and women so large? If the goal of any species is to survive, wouldn’t it make more sense for women to evolve to be closer to men in regards to physical strength as to better protect their children?
Answer: There is an important factor contributing to sexual dimorphism in human beings — food sources. In a hunter/gatherer society, men were the hunters and women were the gatherers. This resulted in specialization in body and brain developerment. Men became bigger and stronger to hunt big game, while women became smaller with less muscle mass than men so they needed less food to survive. Men would go out hunting large game like mammoths, where their much greater upper body strength and targeting ability with spears, not to mention aggressiveness, were paramount. Women would stay close to home with the children and pick berries and nuts, and grains where their better dexterity and colour vision (7% of men are colour blind) helped find them find and gather food. This gave the tribe access to two different sources of food — meat and plants. Men provided the meat, whereas women provided the plant foods. Given the synergy, pairs of men and women formed to have a complete diet for omniverous human beings. Since children are helpless for their first few years, a woman needed a man to help feed and protect her and her children while they were growing, which led to monogamy. In terms of protection, women protected the children and kept them safe, while men protected the whole tribe and did their best to kill large predators. This was best done in large groups, which resulted in them being able to turn off their natural aggressiveness when dealing with women and other men in the same tribe. However in a violent society, men got killed much more often than women, A successful hunter could support many wives, which led to polygamy.

Question: How do you claim crown land in BC?
Answer: You can’t just “claim” Crown land anywhere in Canada. You have to buy it or lease it from the Crown, but in general it is not for sale. The Homestead Act has long since been revoked in BC, and claiming land by Adverse Possession (squatter’s rights) has been extinguished by the Land Titles Act, so your only choices are to buy it from the Crown (which generally does not want to sell it), Lease it, (assuming the Crown wants to lease it to you for some purpose), or License it, in which case your tenancy can be revoked at any time on whim by the BC government. In BC you have the additional complication that the First Nations have first claim on Crown land — in fact the total area of Native land claims in BC exceeds the total area of BC and these claims have not been resolved. First Nations land is not for sale, either, although it can be leased for up to 40 years.

Question: What do I do if I own mineral rights and the oil company refuses to pay the royalties?
Answer: You need to get a lawyer with oil and gas lease experience involved to asses the situation for you. I assume they have an oil lease signed by you. If they don’t, they are trespassing on your land and you can kick them off it, potentially seizing all their equipment on it. This requires a court order. If they have a lease, it should specify a royalty rate, i.e the share of their production that they must give you. If they are not paying the agreed upon royalties, they are in breach of the lease terms and you can sue them and evict them from your land. However, if there is no production at all, the royalties are zero unless otherwise stated. The relevant government oil and gas regulation department might also want to know if an oil company is screwing you out of royalty payments. This depends on the particular government involved. Some are more proactive than others. If the company has working interest partners in the operation, notify them. Not paying the royalties owing will put them in breach of contract with their partners, in which case the partners might take the operation away from them and give the money to you directly. Oil companies take this kind of thing seriously because it could cost them the lease and involve penalties. However, note that the most common reason for not paying the royalties is that the company has run out of cash and is approaching bankruptcy, so even if you do sue, you may get nothing in a lawsuit. They probably owe a lot of money to a lot of other people such as suppliers and banks if they are risking losing their leases. I worked for one oil company in which the most profitable department was Joint Venture Audit. We would send our auditors to a partner company’s office as per the terms of our agreement, the auditors would spend a few weeks digging through their financial records, and come back with a few million dollars in unpaid royalties and costs. Sometimes they had printed the cheque as part of their regular computer run, but didn’t send it until we specifically asked for it. I designed a monthy computer report to compare what companies were paying us, and what they SHOULD be paying us based on their production and our agreement, and if there was a major discrepancy, out went the auditors. I did however have access to data that the average landowner does not.

Question: If the Declaration of Independence was our divorce from the prior legal precedence of the Old World, from what and whom do the legal lawyers of today base their legal precedence?
Answer: The American revolution was not as revolutionary as you seem to think. In fact the new United States officially adopted English Common Law as of 1766, and the precedents in that go back to the Norman French conquest of England in 1066. Since 1766 American Common Law has diverged from other Common Law countries. An example is the distinction between a felony and a misdemeaner, which is an old English categorization of crimes which is still used in the US, but no longer used in the UK, Canada, Australia, etc. This is particularly apparent in real estate law - in fact the phrase real estate comes from Middle English. The word “real” is derived from Latin, meaning existing, actual, or genuine. The word “estate” is an English translation of the Old French word “estat,” meaning status. When you read the title for your land, it may say you have an “Estate in Fee Simple”, which means you have a simple feudal estate. If an oil company leases your land to produce oil, what you give them is not a lease but an old English right called a “profit a prendre” which means the right to take something from your land (i.e. oil) and sell it for their own profit. The judges don’t care what you call it — they will read it and tell you what it is, based on medieval precidents. The US state of Louisiana and the Canadian province of Quebec derive their laws from French Civil Law (Code Napoleon), which makes their law systems quite different than the English Common Law states and provinces. It requires special training for lawyers to practice law there.

Question: Is Imane Khelif a "biological man"?

Question: My husband signed the title to his mother. The deed still in his name. He paid the mortgage & tax. Mom passed away. Now the siblings are interested to sell the house. What’s the law in Florida saying about this situation?

I would speculate that what he did was add his mother to the tltle as “joint tenant with right of survivorship”. This means that they both own the house 50/50 until one of them dies, and then the survivor (your husband in this case) automatically owns the house 100%. Where I live in Alberta this is relatively simple — you send the death certificate to the Land Titles office, they just strike the deceased tenant (tenant = owner) off the title, and there is only one name left on the title, who owns it 100%. This occurs before the will is read, bypasses probate, and is an efficient way of preventing unwanted siblings and offspring from inheriting the property and selling it. If your husband is already paying the mortgage and taxes, nothing changes there. However, things get a little wild and crazy in the real estate business south of the 49th parallel, particularly in Florida where the con men outnumber the gators, so if your in-laws get greedy you might need to get a good lawyer to handle the case for you and make sure all the i’s are dotted and t’s crossed.

Question: What is the difference in working interest and operating rights in an oil and gas lease?
Answer: Working interest and operating interest are more or less the same thing. In a working interest partnership, several companies sign an agreement share the costs of exploration, drilling, and production of the oil and/or gas. As part of their investment, working interest partners receive a share of the net profits of any successful wells. This is in contrast to royalty interests, whose owners receive a share of the profits but pay none of the costs. Typically these parties owned the mineral rights but let the working interest partners develop the lease for them in return for a share of the profits. This is lower risk (zero costs, zero liability) but also lower profit than a working interest in the wells. It is prudent for WI owners to operate through a limited liability company in case of bankruptcy or lawsuit, whereas RI owners can just collect the cheques. There are two types of working interest: operated and non-operated. Operated working interest has a designated operator that makes all operational decisions. The partners vote to see who becomes the lease operator. The WI partners vote to see which will be the operating partner. Typically this is the WI partner with the largest share, but not always. The operating partner charges a share of the often very high costs to the other WI owners… but not the RI owners. A non-operated working interest (NOWI) is a type of working interest in an oil and/or gas lease that does not come with the right to operate the lease.A non-operated WI partner is not involved in daily operations but pays its share of the costs and is consulted on production decisions. Non-operated working interests are typically held by investors who do not have the expertise to operate an oil and gas lease, but still want to participate in the production and profits from the lease.

Question: I split the cost of a fence with my old neighbor. A new neighbor has moved in and is wanting to remove the fence. The fence is entirely on their property. Can they legally do this?
Answer: If you paid for half of the fence, it is 50% your fence, and he can’t tear down your half without your permission. It is what is known in law as a “fixture”, which is to say it is fixed to the ground, and fixtures run with the land, not the owner even if the land changes ownership. Now the law gets tricky here because the previous owner granted you what is known as an “easement” against his property to build your half of of the fence on it. An easement is a legally binding right that grants one party the authority to use another's property for a specific purpose. Again, this right is attached to and runs with the land, not the owner even if the owner changes. A land owner cannot just unilaterally revoke it without a court decision. Easements do not have to be in writing for something as trivial as a fence. A simple handshake will suffice. The original owner granted you the right to build it, so the new owner is stuck with it because that right belongs to the property and not to him. You still have a claim of rights against his property and to interfere with your right to have a fence there is trespass against your rights to his property.

Question: A friend offered to buy my house and let me live in it until I die. Is this risky?

A life estate is an interest in property that lasts only for the life of a specific person, usually the possessor of the estate. The owner of a life estate cannot leave the property to anyone in their will as their interest in the property will terminate at their death. The holder has full rights to possess and use the property until they die, and then the buyer, called the remainderman, will assume full ownership. Keep in mind that this bypasses your will and the transfer of title will happen automatically when you die. You cannot change this by changing your will. The buyer’s name is on the title.

Question: According to RT, the US importing 10,000 barrels of oil from Russia last year (down from 30 million barrels), means that US sanctions have failed?

Name: David Moe
Question: Can you open a bank account for business when you already have one?
Answer: It is quite common for people to have two bank accounts, one personal account and one for their business. This can be done to segregate personal income from business income and simplify the accounting process. For instance, when I was consulting I had my personal account, but I set up my own consulting corporation to receive the bills. I was the sole employee of my corporation, and while I was making only minimum wage, it was making out like a bandit in the stock market with the money it did not pay me, the costs it incurred, and the taxes it didn’t pay. The accounting costs were pretty high, but my accountant assured me it was all legal. It is common for tradesmen to have a numbered company with a separate bank account to charge their business expenses to, separate from their personal accounts for tax purposes. A friend of mine who was a carpenter did this. His company got a lot of discounts on supplies and had a lot of costs for tax purposes. I suspect a lot of lumber he bought went into his own homes, but are the tax people going to count 2x4s? My grandfather was a poor prairie dirt farmer, sold the farm, and bought another one just south of Vancouver to raise chickens and fruit trees. And then Vancouver (which has the highest house prices in Canada) expanded out and overran his farm, so he just sold off lots when he needed money. Being an immigrant farmer with not a lot of education, he thought there must be some kind of law against having that much money, so he kept his money in 8 different bank accounts to hide it from the government.

Name: David Moe
Question: What if a bank has enough credit on its central bank's account to operate normally, but it doesn't have enough cash to give to its customers, where does such a bank get the cash from? Does government print new banknotes and give the bank the cash?
Answer: My wife used to work in a liquor store across the street from a bank. Around Christmas time the bank would run out of cash, so a cashier would run across the street with a cashiers cheque, and buy up all of their surplus cash. And then the customers would walk across the street with their cash and buy liquor with it. It was a circular process. However, banks in the United States order currency and coin from the Federal Reserve (Fed) and deposit excess banknotes back with the Fed. This may take a few days, but if you examine the bank’s rules, you will find that they have a few days to satisfy your demand if the amount exceeds their cash reserves on hand. If all else fails, the government can just print more money.

Name: David Moe
Question: Why do we have coins that are 25 cents instead of 20, and why do we have 20-dollar bills instead of 25?
Answer: Because centuries ago the US used Spanish silver dollars as currency, and to make change they would literally cut them into pieces, called bits, which were worth eight “Reales,” a unit of currency in Spain. The quarter dollar was a convenient unit of currency, worth two bits, so those names of “quarter” and “two bits” are often used to describe the modern 25 cent coin. This continued even after the US started minting its own coins. It is noteworthy that Australia with less history with Spain and Mexico has a 20 cent coin rather than a 25 cent coin. Cutting paper currency into pieces is frowned upon, so it is issued in $1, $2, $5, $10, $20, $50, and $100 bills in the US. Australia has dropped the 1 cent coin and replaced the $1 and $2 bills with coins. Canada has done the same.

Question: Is capitalism like a casino in that it's rigged against the working class? When you job interview they look at your work history in detail and make sure you have experience but they don't make sure your wage covers cost of living.

I know a number of plumbers who started their own plumbing company, and at that point the money started rolling in. However, you have to understand how to keep the books and manage people, which is a barrier for many people. Whining and complaining because you are a loser doesn’t help at all. I started 6 foot below ground as a grave digger to pay for my college degree, and from there the only direction was up. When I got my computer science degree the ladder got really steep, and the 12 hour days a little tough, but the money got better. The world does not owe you a living, so do something useful rather than whatever you do. I could automate your job out of existence, which was my job.

Question: Would it be possible for Canada to double its agricultural output?

Canadian farmers only farm class 1 and 2 farmland, and graze cattle on class 3. Europeans farm what would be considered class 4 farmland, which would be left as forest in Canada. However, the vast majority of this undeveloped land is in Western Canada, where the vast, infertile Canadian Shield ends and the vast, fertile Canadian Prairies begin. About 85% of the country’s agricultural land is in the West, whereas the majority of the population lives in Ontario and Quebec. The fertile land in the West extends nearly up to the Northwest Territories, whereas in the East it ends at the Shield. Question: Can my minor daughter with US Citizen move back to Canada permanently with me if I have Canadian Citizenship? Will she be able to go to elementary school without any problem? Will apply for her citizenship while in Canada.
Answer: If you had Canadian citizenship when she was born, she has Canadian citizenship by the rule of Jus sanguinis (right of blood) and is thus a dual American/Canadian citizen. If she was born in Canada she has Canadian citizenship by the rule of Jus soli (right of the soil). It is quite easy for Americans to acquire Canadian citizenship without knowing it. You might want to contact Canadian immigration to clarify this situation and get the proper paperwork. If you did not have Canadian citizenship when she was born, you need to bring her in under another category. If she does have Canadian citizenship or permanent residency she will automatically be allowed to go to a Canadian elementary school, more or less for free.

Question: US: Vancouver is above US but not very much colder than many US cities. why?
Answer: The distance between Seattle and Vancouver is only 120 miles (200 km). That is not enough to produce a major difference in climate. Both are exposed to the moderating effect of the Pacific Ocean and thus have much warmer winters and cooler summers than cities further inland which have a continental climate. Toronto is 60 miles (100 km) north of Buffalo, NY, again not enough to make a major difference in temperature. Both are under the moderating effect of Lake Ontario, the difference being that Toronto is in a snow shadow, while Buffalo gets hit by lake effect snow and is in a snow belt, so it gets far more snow. You need to look at wind patterns, water bodies, and ocean currents to figure out cities’ climates. Latitude is not the only factor.

Question: The United States unilaterally announced an expansion of its continental shelf sovereignty claims in the Arctic Ocean, covering an ocean area of approximately 1 million square kilometers. Is this reasonable? Why no country opposes？

Question: Why did the new light rail chose standard rail gauge 750 volt pantograph wire instead of the existing legacy streetcar system using custom rail with trolley pole 600 volt wire?
Answer: The overwhelming advantage of standard guage rail is that it is standard. They can use standard railway equipment such as maintenance equipment and even diesel locomotives on the same track. If it is nonstandard gauge, they have to build their own maintenance equpment, which is much more expensive. The vehicles are also more expensive since they have to be custom built. The voltage is immaterial since they can order vehicles with either 600 or 750 volt traction motors. 750 volts is more efficient. Pantographs are much more reliable than trolley poles. Light rail transit (LRT) is characterized by a combination of tram and rapid transit features. It is very flexible and can operate as anything from a tram to a light metro train, underground, elevated, but usually at grade since that is cheaper. While its rolling stock is similar to a traditional tram, it operates at a higher capacity and speed, and can be used in muliple unit mode with a variable number of vehicles from 1 to 4 or 5. I rode the LRT in Calgary for years, and they started off in tram mode and ran it down the middle of a downtown street. As it expanded, they kept adding more and more cars until now they are running 4 car trains with 1000 passengers aboard. The last line they built had the city’s first elevated station and first underground station. The next line will have to go underground because they are running out of street space for the surface system. It is however unbelievable how many 1000 passenger trains you can run down the middle of a narrow downtown street per hour with no fuss or bother. It is equivalent to a 16 lane freeway.

Question: Why have gas prices gone under 3 dollars? Have we begged the Saudis again or are we emptying our strategic oil reserves?

Question: I brush and floss my teeth everyday but still get cavities. I noticed people in third world countries get less cavities, why is that? Does their food contain probotic cultures?
Answer: Prior to the invention of agriculture, almost nobody got cavities because they got very little carbohydrates and sugar in their diets. After agriculture was introduced, the carbohydrates in grain caused cavities in people’s teeth. Archeologists can date the arrival of agriculture in various regions by looking at the teeth on old skeletons to see if they had cavities. After sugar started being produced in industrial quantities, the number of cavities increased. Studies of old skeleteons show that on British naval ships, the officers had far more cavities than the common sailors because they could afford sugar in their food. People in third world countries may have fewer cavities because they don’t get much sugar in their food. The bacteria in your mouth that thrive on carbohydrates and sugars generate acid that eats through the enamel on your teeth. Your first line of defense against that, other than cutting down on carbohydrates and eliminating sugar, is to have fluoride in your water, which will strengthen your tooth enamel by changing its chemical constitution. Your second line of defense is your dentist, who will recommend a fluoride toothpaste.

Question: I have noticed on British TV shows that some very old homes built just off the street that they front on have entrances that are below the street level. Is this because the height of the street was raised over the centuries?
Answer: Old houses sink into the ground, or from another perspective, the ground level rises. I once owned a century-old house, and it was obvious that the house had sunk below street level since it was built. I had to excavate dirt from around the house to keep water from running in, and I was thinking of putting it on jacks, raising it a couple of feet, and pouring a cap on the concrete basement. In London, which is 2000 years old, the difference can be incredible. The ground level has risen 20 feet since it started. I looked at one old building, and its main storey was now about 10 feet below street level. They just built a new entrance into second storey. It is primarily caused by dust falling out of the air, or grass clippings that are not removed when the lawn is cut. The city should strip the surface pavement off the street before repaving it to prevent the street from rising above the house levels. Rome has risen 45 feet since it was founded, and there are entire old cities buried under the current one.

Name: David Moe
Question: What was the rule of Ukrainians in the development of agriculture in Canada?

The Parkland Belt of the prairies is very similar to Ukraine and has some of the best soil in Canada. The Canadian government wanted new agricultural immigrants to populate Canada's vast prairies, and gave them 160 acres of free homestead land, but English immigrants didn’t know how to farm under such cold conditions and most of them were industrial workers. Clifford Sifton, Canada’s Minister of Immigration, famously said “I think that a stalwart peasant in a sheepskin coat, born to the soil, whose forefathers have been farmers for ten generations, with a stout wife and a half-dozen children, is good quality.” After WW1 subsequent waves of Ukrainian immigrants settled in urban areas because all the good free agricultural land was gone. There are now 1.4 million Ukranian descendants in Canada, the third largest Ukranian population outside Ukraine and Russia, and the number is increasing rapidly because of the war in Ukraine.

Question: Is it true that a very well done steak is the best kind of steak?

Question: Why does cheese cost many times more to produce here in Canada than it does in the US? What goes into the cost inputs here in Canada that doesn't go into the cost inputs in the US? Is it labor, interest costs or something else?
