Question: There are no term time limits for Canadian politicians, including the Prime Minister. Trudeau's latest win marks his third term in office as Prime Minister. Should Canada impose a term limit on the position of Prime Minister? For Cabinet Ministers?
Answer: There are no terms for Canadian politicians, so the idea of term limits is foreign. They serve as long as the voters keep electing them (elections must occur at least every 5 years). Prime Ministers serve as long as they have the confidence of Parliament and the people, and can be ousted at any time without any such formality as impeachment. Unlike the US, it is up to the people how long a politician serves, which in my opinion is a better system. Unlike the US, Canadian voters feel free to change party allegencies between elections, and often vote for different parties in federal and provincial elections. The longest serving Prime Minister was William Lyon Mackenzie King for three non-consecutive terms from 1921 to 1926, 1926 to 1930, and 1935 to 1948. — a total of 21 years and 154 days in office. He was lucky enough to be voted out of office in 1930, so he could blame the Depression on the Conservatives, and then was voted back in 1935 so he could manage WW2.

Question: Why doesn’t the United States have a $15.00 a hour federal minimum wage unlike Canada?
Answer: There is a federal minimum wage in Canada of $16.65, but the Government of Canada has the constitutional authority to set minimum wages only for federal public servants and workers in industries under federal regulation, such as banks, airlines, and railways. Minimum wages for other workers are controlled by the provincial governments and range from $13 to $16. The federal government cannot override these wages because it does not have constitutional authority to do so. However, unlike US states, Canadian provinces cooperate with each other in setting minimum wages and working standards, so they are all more or less the same, regardless of which political party is in power. There are a lot more political parties in Canada than in the US, so it is up to the voters to decide. Not so much in the US which is becoming less of a democracy all the time.

Question: Why is life in Canada better for the least affluent in Canada whilst in America life is worse for the least affluent in America?

My university degrees were heavily subsidized by the government, and I went for a couple of years sleeping on a cot in a basement because I couldn’t afford a bed, and walked to university because I couldn’t afford bus fare, but eventually after getting my STEM degrees, I got to the point where I owned four houses and gave another one away because I didn’t need it. Question: Newspaper says to expect 50¢ to $1.00 per gallon increase while refineries change to their winter formula. This increase didn't used to happen 20 years ago. Why is there an increase during the transition?

Question: Given that the USA lose millions of dollars every year since the EU, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, plus most other countries trade in the metric system, could the US government use force to make those countries shift to Imperial?
Answer: No, because each country has control over its own unit system and another country cannot force them to change. On the other hand, other countries can ban imports which are not on the metric system —the international system (System International or SI) which is recognized worldwide, including in the US. Metric units are legal in the US, while US conventional units are legal in no other country. Even the British Imperial system is different from the US conventional system, because none of the liquid units like the pint, quart, and gallon are the same — they were 20% bigger in the UK and Commonwealth countries. This caused huge problems in Canada which is why we switched to the metric system (SI). Americans suffer a huge amount of hubris on this and other topics, which is why they get into so much trouble in other countries.

Question: How do the Dutch feel about having objectively the worst cuisine in the world?

Pickled fish seems to be somewhat controversial in the UK but I very much like it, as do many people in Northern Europe. They ate what they could grow or fish out of the ocean, or get from their cows. Hollandse Nieuwe (Dutch new herring) is raw herring is served together with chopped raw onions and gherkins. Stamppot is a dish of mashed potatoes combined with root vegetables, like turnip, carrot and onion. Pannenkoeken is Dutch pancakes topped with sweet or savory ingredients; such as bacon, salmon, apple, cheese, chocolate, powdered sugar, and stroop (a treacly Dutch syrup). It is not Italy or Spain, after all, they didn’t have herbs growing wild, and they don’t eat snails and frogs like the French do. If you are travelling, you should eat like the locals do, and it will usually be great. I have had Cuy (Guinea Pig) in Peru, which is good, and Peking duck in China, which is an experience. Some of the Norwegian food I am used to will cause gagging in people who have never smelled lutefisk (dried cod fish soaked in lye and boiled) but in my family it was a Christmas treat. Norwegian brown cheese is made from whey which in other countries would be thrown away. The Swedes go us one better and have food (Surströmming — Swedish for 'sour herring') in cans that should only be opened outside downwind from the house. It is banned in the US because the Americans think it is rotten fish. I think Dutch food is a step or two up from that. Most Scandinavians have settled on pizza as their favourite dish.

Question: Why is Canada so green north of Edmonton? Shouldn't the rain-shadow of the Rockies make it as dry as eastern Montana?
Answer: It is because of global wind circulation patterns. This is an oversimplication, but there are three main global wind patterns, the Ferrel Cell, the Hadley Cell, and the Polar Cell in both hemispheres both north and south of the equator. The Ferrel Cell picks up moisture at about 30 degrees north and south latitude, and deposits it at the equator, which is why most of the world’s deserts are at about 30 degrees and south of the equator, and the equator is mostly tropical rain forest. The Hadley Cell picks up moisture at about 30 degrees north/south - hence deserts, and deposits it at about 60 degrees north/south. The Polar Cell picks up moisture from the poles and deposits it at about 60 degrees, too. In most of both the US and Canada, climates are driven by the Hadley Cell. If you will note, the 30th parallel runs through the US (which has some big deserts), and the 60th parallel runs through Canada, so northern Canada is much wetter then the southern US. Edmonton is at 53.5 degrees, so it only gets wetter and greener north of that. The Earth is also rotating, so the coreolis effect adds an additional complication. Winds in the Ferrel Cell region blow from east to west (the easterly trade winds), those in the Haldley Cell blow from west to east (the prevailing westerlies), and the polar easterlies blow from east to west. Since the Rocky Mountains in western Montana are very high, the prevailing westerlies drop most of their moisture on the west slopes of the Rockies, leaving the plains in eastern Montana very dry. OTOH, the Rockies west of Edmonton are much lower, so the winds drop their moisture on the very fertile farmland around Edmonton (the Parkland Belt). Further north the mountains are even lower, so the winds drop too much rain for most agriculture, and so there are a lot of green trees.

In the other colonies that later made up Canada, the judges simply made it impossible for Americans to reclaim their slaves by insisting they produce a legal title document, which none of them had. The Southern American colonies had to pass their own laws to make it legal in the US. Some people quote the date of 1834 for the end of slavery in the British Empire, but that was for the colonies which had not already abolished slavery. Britain and Canada had made it illegal long before that date. It took until 1865 for the United States to abolish slavery. Prior to the Civil War in the US in 1861–1865, the refusal of Canada to return slaves to the US resulted in the Underground Railroad, which moved slaves from the US to Canada via routes supported by anti-slavery groups. There were no particular laws against black people immigrating to Canada, and once they got there they were home free. Slave owners trying to capture them and return them to the US could be charged with kidnapping. After slavery was abolished in the US in 1865, many of the former slaves returned to the US on their own initiative.

Question: How does Alberta beef compare to Texas beef?
Answer: The main difference is that Alberta beef is generally grass fed, while Texas beef is generally corn fed. The reason is that it is very difficult to grow corn at the latitude of Alberta — there are not enough “corn heat days”, meaning it is not hot enough for long enough to grow feed corn, although there is some sweet corn grown. The result is that Alberta beef is leaner, and in my opinion, more flavourful. Grass is natural cattle food, while corn is not. Cattle never used to eat corn before the Americas were discovered, and their digestive systems are not designed for it. It is missing a number of nutrients and a lot of it goes straight through the cow without being digested. It is beef from unhappy cattle who never get out to graze. Having grown up in Alberta, my first taste of Texas beef was very disappointing. I began to realize why Americans always used steak sauce, whereas we never used it back on the ranch in Alberta. And we used to buy and sell beef by the half cow, which made it much cheaper. Question: How do Canadians spell ‘sulfur’?
Answer: Canadians use the older English spelling of “sulphur”, derived from Greek. The ph represents the Greek letter phi. Americans decided to Americanize it by calling it “sulfur”, but Canadians declined to follow their lead. I once read the Environmental Impact study in the US for the “Sulphur Creek Sulfur Plant”.
